title: ICSE Class 8 physics & chemistry | Part -ii | matter , physical quantities and measurements, physical and chemical changes
description: ICSE Class 8 physics & chemistry | Part -ii | matter , physical quantities and measurements, physical and chemical changes
subject: physics

questions.question: A substance 'X' has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. When heated, its intermolecular space increases considerably until it completely fills any closed container it is placed in. What states of matter are represented before and after heating respectively?
questions.explanation: Liquids have a fixed volume but no fixed shape. Upon heating to their boiling point, they become gases, which fill the entire volume of the container due to maximized intermolecular space.
questions.hint: Think about which state of matter has a definite volume but no definite shape.

questions.question: During a laboratory experiment, a student heats a mixture of sodium chloride and ammonium chloride in a china dish covered with an inverted funnel. Which physical process will help separate the ammonium chloride?
questions.explanation: Ammonium chloride directly converts from a solid to a gas on heating without passing through the liquid state, a process known as sublimation. Sodium chloride does not sublime.
questions.hint: Look for the process where a solid turns directly into a vapor.

questions.question: An empty density bottle weighs 22 g. When filled completely with water, it weighs 50 g. When filled completely with an unknown liquid 'L', it weighs 43 g. What is the relative density of the liquid 'L'?
questions.explanation: Mass of water = 50 g - 22 g = 28 g. Mass of liquid = 43 g - 22 g = 21 g. Relative density = (Mass of liquid) / (Mass of equal volume of water) = 21 / 28 = 0.75.
questions.hint: Relative Density = Mass of Liquid / Mass of equal volume of Water.

questions.question: Based on the data in the previous question (empty bottle = 22 g, with water = 50 g, with liquid = 43 g), what is the density of the liquid 'L' in SI units (kg/m³)?
questions.explanation: The relative density is 0.75. Density in CGS units (g/cm³) is numerically equal to relative density, so it is 0.75 g/cm³. To convert to SI units (kg/m³), multiply by 1000. Thus, 0.75 x 1000 = 750 kg/m³.
questions.hint: Multiply the density in CGS units by 1000 to get SI units.

questions.question: A piece of iron of volume 30 cm³ has a mass of 234 g. What will happen if this iron piece is dropped into a beaker containing a liquid of density 8.0 g/cm³?

options.text: It will float with half its volume submerged.
It will float completely submerged just below the surface.
It will sink to the bottom.
It will float with a small portion above the surface.

questions.explanation: Density of iron = Mass / Volume = 234 / 30 = 7.8 g/cm³. Since the density of iron (7.8 g/cm³) is less than the density of the liquid (8.0 g/cm³), the iron piece will float.
questions.hint: Compare the density of the object with the density of the fluid.

questions.question: Case Study: Ria took an empty density bottle and weighed it. She then filled it with a liquid 'X' and weighed it again. She emptied it, dried it thoroughly, and filled it with water to find the bottle's capacity. Why is it necessary to dry the density bottle completely before filling it with a different liquid?

options.text: To increase the volume of the density bottle.
To prevent the glass from cracking due to temperature differences.
To avoid mixing of liquids which would alter the mass and density calculations.
To decrease the relative density of the new liquid.

questions.explanation: Any remaining water droplets will mix with the new liquid, changing its true mass and volume within the bottle, leading to an inaccurate determination of its density.
questions.hint: Think about purity and how leftover moisture affects the overall mass.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of relative density?
questions.explanation: Relative density is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water at 4°C. Since it is a ratio of two identical physical quantities, the units cancel out.
questions.hint: It is a pure ratio.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the change in temperature when ice at -10°C is heated continuously until it becomes steam at 110°C?

options.text: The temperature rises constantly without stopping.
The temperature rises, remains constant at 0°C, rises again, and remains constant at 100°C.
The temperature remains horizontal and flat throughout the heating process.

questions.explanation: Temperature rises until the melting point (0°C), stays constant during melting due to latent heat of fusion, rises again until the boiling point (100°C), and stays constant during boiling due to latent heat of vaporization.
questions.hint: Phase changes occur at constant temperatures.

questions.question: When a solid is heated, it expands. Assuming the mass remains constant, how does this thermal expansion affect the density of the solid?

options.text: The density first decreases then increases.

questions.explanation: Density is mass divided by volume. As the solid expands on heating, its volume increases. Since mass is constant, an increase in volume results in a decrease in density.
questions.hint: Density is inversely proportional to volume.

questions.question: A 50 cm³ density bottle weighs 30 g when empty. It is filled with a liquid of relative density 1.2. What will be the total mass of the density bottle filled with this liquid?
questions.explanation: Volume of liquid = 50 cm³. Density of liquid = 1.2 g/cm³ (since RD is 1.2). Mass of liquid = Density x Volume = 1.2 x 50 = 60 g. Total mass = Mass of bottle + Mass of liquid = 30 g + 60 g = 90 g.
questions.hint: Find the mass of the liquid first using its volume and density.

questions.question: Burning of a candle is considered both a physical and a chemical change. Which part of this process specifically represents the chemical change?

options.text: Combustion of the wax vapors producing carbon dioxide and water vapor.

questions.explanation: Combustion produces entirely new substances (carbon dioxide, water vapor, soot) with properties different from wax, making it a chemical change. Melting and vaporization are changes of state (physical changes).
questions.hint: Look for the step where new chemical substances are formed.

questions.question: A student adds a spoonful of ammonium chloride to a beaker of water and stirs. He notices that the beaker becomes quite cold to the touch. What type of change has occurred?
questions.explanation: Dissolving ammonium chloride in water absorbs heat from the surroundings (making the beaker cold), so it is an endothermic process. It is a physical change because the original solid can be recovered by evaporating the water.
questions.hint: A dropping temperature indicates heat absorption, and dissolving is generally a reversible process.

questions.question: Rusting of iron is a significant problem in coastal areas. Which two conditions are absolutely essential for the rusting of iron to take place?
questions.explanation: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. For iron to react and form rust, it must be exposed to both oxygen (from the air) and moisture (water). If either is absent, rusting will not occur.
questions.hint: Think about what specific components in damp air react with metals.

questions.question: Magnetizing a piece of iron by rubbing it with a bar magnet is classified as a physical change. Why is this so?

options.text: Because energy is released in the form of heat.
Because a new permanent substance called "magnetic iron" is formed.
Because no new substance is formed and the chemical composition remains the same.
Because the change is completely irreversible.

questions.explanation: During magnetization, the magnetic domains within the iron simply align. No new chemical substance is created, and the iron retains its original chemical properties. The process is also temporary and reversible.
questions.hint: Consider whether the actual chemical formula of the iron changes.

questions.question: Case Study: During a science fair, a volcano model is activated by mixing baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) and vinegar (acetic acid). The mixture foams up rapidly, spilling over the edges of the model. Which characteristic of a chemical change is predominantly observed here?

options.text: Change of state from solid to liquid

questions.explanation: The reaction between baking soda and vinegar produces carbon dioxide gas, which causes the rapid bubbling and foaming. This evolution of gas is a strong visual indicator of a chemical change.
questions.hint: Bubbles and foam are visual evidence of a specific phase of matter escaping.

questions.question: Curdling of milk is considered a chemical change, whereas boiling of milk is considered a physical change. What is the primary reason for this distinction?

options.text: Curdling changes the physical state of the milk, while boiling does not.
Curdling produces lactic acid and alters the molecular structure irreversibly, while boiling only temporarily changes the temperature.
Curdling requires heat, while boiling can happen at room temperature.
Boiled milk tastes sour, while curdled milk tastes sweet.

questions.explanation: Curdling involves bacterial action (or addition of an acid) that changes lactose into lactic acid, forming a new substance irreversibly. Boiling simply heats the milk without altering its fundamental chemical composition.
questions.hint: Think about which process creates a permanently different substance.

questions.question: Which of the following demonstrates an application of the high compressibility of gases based on the kinetic theory of matter?

options.text: Water taking the shape of a glass.
Iron expanding in the summer heat.
CNG (Compressed Natural Gas) stored in cylinders for use as vehicle fuel.
Ice floating on the surface of a lake.

questions.explanation: Gases have very large intermolecular spaces, allowing them to be compressed into much smaller volumes under high pressure. This property allows large amounts of CNG to be stored in small cylinders.
questions.hint: Look for the application that implies fitting a large volume into a tight space.

questions.question: An irregular solid object is lowered into a measuring cylinder containing 40 ml of water. The water level rises to 65 ml. If the mass of the solid is 200 g, what is its density?
questions.explanation: Volume of the solid = Final volume - Initial volume = 65 ml - 40 ml = 25 ml (or 25 cm³). Density = Mass / Volume = 200 g / 25 cm³ = 8.0 g/cm³.
questions.hint: Find the volume of the solid using the displacement method first.

questions.question: When silver nitrate solution is added to sodium chloride solution, a white solid instantly forms in the liquid. What is the term for this characteristic of a chemical change?
questions.explanation: A solid that forms and settles out of a liquid mixture during a chemical reaction is called a precipitate. In this specific case, silver chloride precipitates out.
questions.hint: What do we call an insoluble solid that emerges from a liquid solution?

questions.question: A student weighs an empty density bottle and finds it is 15 g. He fills it completely with liquid A (density = 0.8 g/cm³) and it weighs 55 g. He cleans it and fills it completely with liquid B (density = 1.2 g/cm³). What will be the mass of the density bottle when filled with liquid B?
questions.explanation: First, find the volume of the bottle. Mass of liquid A = 55 g - 15 g = 40 g. Volume = Mass / Density = 40 / 0.8 = 50 cm³. Next, find the mass of liquid B. Mass = Density x Volume = 1.2 x 50 = 60 g. Finally, total mass = Mass of bottle + Mass of liquid B = 15 g + 60 g = 75 g.
questions.hint: Find the internal volume of the density bottle using Liquid A first.
